entities.name: Henry, Count of Monte Sant'Angelo
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Henry, Count of Monte Sant'Angelo, a prominent Norman lord in Southern Italy, wielded considerable influence over the Gargano Peninsula from November 1081 until his death on December 28, 1102. As a nephew of the formidable Robert Guiscard and a vassal initially under the Principality of Capua, Henry’s career unfolded amidst the complex, often volatile, political landscape of Norman Apulia during a period marked by consolidation and internecine strife. His strategic position, with his primary seat at Foggia, made him a pivotal figure in the regional power struggles between the Dukes of Apulia and the Princes of Capua, embodying the semi-independent spirit of many Norman magnates.

Henry's tenure was characterized by a series of strategic alliances and open rebellions against ducal authority. He initially swore fealty to Jordan I of Capua and later to Richard II, aligning himself with the Capuan princes against the succession claims of Roger Borsa, Duke of Apulia. This opposition was most pronounced in 1083, when Henry, alongside other rebellious barons, challenged Roger Borsa’s control over Apulia, leveraging his fortified territories on the Gargano. He also provided crucial support to Bohemond I of Antioch, his cousin and Robert Guiscard’s eldest son, during Bohemond’s early struggles for power against Roger Borsa, further destabilizing ducal authority and illustrating the fragmented nature of Norman rule.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Henry's actions as a powerful, rebellious count significantly destabilized the Duchy of Apulia, challenging ducal authority and contributing to the fragmented political landscape of Southern Italy before its eventual unification. His career provides a clear example of the struggles for power between centralizing Norman rulers and their semi-independent vassals.
